Theme

Conversation, family & daily routines

what a shame! phrase

also what a pity!, shame on you!, that’s a darn shame, what an outrage!

classical

Ter. Ph. 4.3.9: facinus indignum, sīc circumīrī (Lewis & Short s.v. circumeō)
Plaut. Men. 5.7.17 (Lewis & Short s.v. dēripiō)
Traupman 107: what a shame!, facinus indignum! or ō rem indignam!

Facinus indignum!

exclamation: nominative or accusative

what a shame! what an outrage!

(vōx cōmica: Plaut., Ter.)

Literally “an unworthy deed!”, often followed by the accusative and infinitive of what is outrageous.

Other words

  • Ō rem indignam! — what a shame!

    exclamatory accusative · also used · classical · Cic. Att. 13.35.1: ō rem indignam! gentīlis tuus urbem auget; Traupman 107: what a shame!, ō rem indignam!

    Built like ō audāciam!, with the exclamatory accusative; Cicero opens a letter to Atticus with it.

  • Edepol facinus improbum! — that’s a darn shame!

    also used · modern · Traupman 107: that’s a darn shame, edepol facinus improbum

    Traupman’s phrase; edepol, “by Pollux”, is the comic oath. Every word is classical; we have found no classical instance of the phrase.

  • Prō pudor! — shame on you! oh, the shame!

    also used · classical · Petr. 81; Mart. 10.68.6 (Lewis & Short s.v. pudor); Traupman 107: shame on you!, prō pudor!; Traupman 258

    Lewis & Short’s instances are all post-Augustan (Petronius, Statius, Martial).

See also cheeky, I’m ashamed.
